lesson.title: Manage food and bathing-facility hygiene
lesson.reading: しょくひんとよくじょうのえいせいをかんりする

objectives.text: Explain HACCP planning, action, records and review
Distinguish bacterial and viral prevention principles
Check the conditions for refrigeration, thawing and bath disinfection

sections.title: Connect plans to actual work and records
sections.body: In food-handling operations, identify hazards through HACCP-based management, establish a hygiene plan and communicate necessary procedures to employees. Record checks such as temperatures and cleaning and review whether the plan and procedures work. Following public health center guidance, managers should check that staff understand what to do, when, against which standard and how to respond to abnormalities. Never invent measurement values simply to fill in records. When processes or equipment change, check whether plans need revision.

sections.title: Manage refrigeration and thawing by food and facility conditions
sections.body: Do not merely look at a refrigerator display: check temperature using the method in the facility plan and report abnormalities. The textbook mentions 2–5°C, but do not treat this as a nationwide universal standard that overrides each food’s storage requirements and process conditions. If a reading is outside the applicable limit, consult the responsible person about causes and handling of the food. Thaw frozen food by an approved method suitable for the food and task rather than leaving it at room temperature for long periods. Cooling does not necessarily make contaminated food safe again.

sections.title: Do not describe bacteria and viruses identically
sections.body: For bacterial food poisoning, consider preventing contamination, limiting multiplication and reducing the organisms through appropriate treatment. Viruses do not multiply in food, so “prevent multiplication” does not apply in the same sense. For viruses, prevent introduction, prevent spread and food contamination, and use necessary heating or other appropriate controls. Learn norovirus, Salmonella and enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157 as examples, but do not limit each cause to one food. Do not identify the cause solely from symptoms or food appearance; pass information to the responsible person and public health center as appropriate. To distinguish examples: norovirus is a virus, whereas Salmonella and O157 are bacteria. The listed bivalves, eggs, meat and vegetables do not restrict a cause to a single food. Norovirus can reach food through infected food handlers’ hands as well as contaminated bivalves. Eggs and meat are checks for Salmonella; meat and vegetable contamination also matter for enterohemorrhagic E. coli. After matching names to food examples, consider how to prevent transfer to other foods through hands and utensils. Do not judge everything safe merely because eggs are absent.

sections.title: Do not judge bath disinfection by appearance alone
sections.body: Clear-looking water does not remove the need for hygiene management in recirculating baths. Staff must continue cleaning, disinfection, water-quality checks and records appropriate to facility conditions. Even with chlorine-based agents, water characteristics, pH, equipment and materials affect the method and effectiveness. Managers should check public health guidance, local ordinances and current management guidance, and ensure staff understand measurement and abnormality responses. “Add chlorine periodically” is not a complete operational procedure. Do not change chemical quantities or concentrations based only on experience; follow approved instructions.

sections.title: Manage equipment for broad usability
sections.body: Universal design at Level 2 is not limited to supplying a separate tool for a particular person. It aims for facilities and products usable by many people regardless of age, sex or disability. When someone reports a difficulty, confirm their usage situation and facility constraints and refer the issue to the improvement team. After changes, review guidance, cleaning and maintenance as well. Check actual use rather than judging only safety, hygiene or usability in isolation.

terms.reading: えいせいかんりけいかく
terms.meaning: A plan specifying hygiene-management methods, standards and related arrangements

terms.reading: じゅんかんしきよくそう
terms.meaning: A bath that recirculates water for use

example.situation: The facility installs a new refrigerator and bath-disinfection system.
steps: Check approved management conditions for each food and item of equipment.
Explain measurement, records and reporting of abnormalities to staff.
Review subsequent records and conditions and revise the plan if needed.

practice.prompt: Correct these statements with reasons and conditions: “Refrigeration stops viruses multiplying in food”; “Every food is safe at 2–5°C”; “Adding chlorine completes hot-spring management.”
expectedPoints: Viruses do not multiply in food
Food-specific storage conditions and contamination prevention
Baths also require measurement, records and cleaning appropriate to conditions

questions.prompt: Which action follows HACCP-based hygiene management?
choices: Keep no records if there is no problem
Record guessed temperatures without measuring
Share the plan, implement it, record and verify results, and revise when necessary
Do not check procedures after equipment changes
questions.explanation: Hygiene management links planning to implementation, records and verification of effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Which statement about viral food poisoning is appropriate?
choices: Viruses multiply in food, so refrigeration alone completes prevention
Prevent introduction, spread and attachment to food, and carry out necessary treatment
Contamination is always visible
Viruses multiply exactly like bacteria
questions.explanation: Viruses do not multiply in food. Preventing introduction and spread of contamination is important.

choices: Use one temperature for every food
Refrigeration always makes contaminated food safe
Watch the display without reporting abnormalities
Check food- and process-specific limits, measure and respond to abnormalities
questions.explanation: Do not treat one textbook number as a universal standard; use a plan appropriate to the food and process.

questions.prompt: Which management of a recirculating bath is appropriate?
choices: Continue cleaning, disinfection, measurement and records appropriate to conditions
Do not test if the water looks clear
Add chemicals by experience alone
No management is needed after one disinfection
questions.explanation: Observe water and equipment conditions and follow public health guidance and facility procedures.

choices: Design only for a particular age group
Aim for usability by many people regardless of age or disability
Prioritize only low cost
Do not ask about users’ difficulties
questions.explanation: Aim for facilities and products that more people can use, without restricting the users assumed.

questions.prompt: Which approach to thawing frozen food is appropriate?
choices: Frozen food may be left at room temperature for a long time
Use an approved method suited to the food and task and avoid leaving it at room temperature
A display reading makes procedure checks unnecessary
Cooling it again always makes it safe
questions.explanation: Check thawing methods for the food and process. Avoid prolonged room-temperature exposure and do not treat cooling as a safety guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which statement about microorganisms and food examples is appropriate?
choices: Norovirus is restricted to bivalves and cannot pass from hands to food
Removing eggs eliminates food-poisoning checks
All causative microorganisms multiply identically in food
Consider bivalves and food handlers’ hands for norovirus, and eggs or meat for Salmonella
questions.explanation: Food examples guide checks rather than restricting a cause to one food. Consider hand and utensil contamination and distinguish viruses from bacteria.

questions.prompt: Which three viewpoints help prevent bacterial food poisoning?
choices: Prevent contamination, suppress multiplication and reduce organisms through appropriate treatment
Refrigeration always reverses contamination
Always let viruses multiply in food before controlling them
One cleaning removes the need for storage and heating controls
questions.explanation: Distinguish contamination prevention, multiplication control and necessary treatment. Viruses do not multiply in food, so the bacterial explanation cannot simply be transferred.

questions.prompt: What is appropriate when considering enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157?
choices: Check only meat, never vegetables
Consider contamination of meat and vegetables and avoid transfer from hands and utensils to food
Guarantee no contamination from appearance alone
Knowing the name removes the need to check handling
questions.explanation: Do not limit the examples to one food. Consider contamination through hands and utensils and appropriate handling.

questions.prompt: A public health center gives food-hygiene guidance. What should the manager do?
choices: Check it, reflect it in plans and procedures, share with staff and connect it to implementation, records and review
Only change how records look
Continue old methods unconditionally without informing staff
Record guessed values that were not measured
questions.explanation: Connect official guidance to workplace planning and action. Receiving guidance alone does not complete the work.
